~2 Holmberg radii. Using H I images and new photometry, we build three component models of the 
mass distribution: a luminous disk with a constant ^/L, a gas disk whose mass is determined by H I 
flux, and a dark halo. This galaxy is remarkable in a number of ways: ( 1 ) the mass-to-light ratio is 56, 
(2) the ratio of gas mass to blue luminosity is 3.7 in solar units, (3) it is the smallest galaxy where the

all comparable to values found for bright galaxies. An extrapolation of the L-v relation for bright disk 
galaxies (L oc v^ax ) correctly predicts the rotation velocity at the Holmberg radius. The velocity separa- 
tion of it and its companion supports the L oc Ay8 scaling found for the velocity differences in binary 
pairs of galaxies. The constraints are robust to gross changes and are the best current limits on the phase

VAN GORKOMb) Department of Astronomy, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027 Received 1 June 1989; revised 24 October 1989 ABSTRACT DDO 170 is a dwarf galaxy of absolute magnitude MB = — 15.15 with a rotation curve measured to ~2 Holmberg radii. Using H I images and new photometry, we build three component models of the mass distribution: a luminous disk with a constant ^/L, a gas disk whose mass is determined by H I flux, and a dark halo. This galaxy is remarkable in a number of ways: ( 1 ) the mass-to-light ratio is 56, (2) the ratio of gas mass to blue luminosity is 3.7 in solar units, (3) it is the smallest galaxy where the basic halo parameters (core radius rc and asymptotic velocity vmax) have been determined by fitting detailed mass models, (4) it has a companion with a projected separation of 62 kpc and a line-of-sight velocity difference of 85 km s~ ^ Over one-third of the “visible” mass of this galaxy is in the form of gas. In the best-fit model of the rotation curve, the halo parameters are rc = 2.4 kpc and vmax — 73 km s-1. The “minimum phase density” model has rc =4.1 kpc, vmax = 79 km s-1. The central density of the halo, its density at the Holmberg radius and the ratio of light-to-dark mass at the Holmberg radius are all comparable to values found for bright galaxies. An extrapolation of the L-v relation for bright disk galaxies (L oc v^ax ) correctly predicts the rotation velocity at the Holmberg radius. The velocity separa- tion of it and its companion supports the L oc Ay8 scaling found for the velocity differences in binary pairs of galaxies. The constraints are robust to gross changes and are the best current limits on the phase density of dark matter. The minimum mass to bind the companion is 5.2X ICP^q, while the standard statistical mass estimator yields 5.2 X 10n^o. While the luminosity of DDO 170 is ~ 1% of L* (the characteristic luminosity defined by the luminosity function), its total mass is nearly the same as that of an L* galaxy. I. INTRODUCTION Observations of spiral galaxies have firmly established the existence of dark matter, but much less is known about the distribution of mass in ellipticals and dwarf galaxies. Dwarf galaxies are candidates for detailed analysis of some of the unresolved questions concerning the nature of dark halos: What is the luminosity dependence of the ratio of light to dark mass? What is the smallest turnover velocity of a rotation curve? What is the smallest halo core radius? What is the smallest mass of a dark halo? What is the highest phase density? Is the law of gravity correct (Lake 1989b)? Over the last several years, there has been mounting evi- dence that even the most extreme dwarf galaxies contain an appreciable amount of dark matter: ( 1 ) the large velocity dispersions seen in the star-by-star observations by Aaron- son ( 1983); (2) their large tidal radii (recently reexamined by Faber and Lin 1983 ) ; ( 3 ) the large velocity separations of pairs of dwarf irregulars (Lake and Schommer 1984). We observed eight dwarf irregulars at the VLA in October 1984 to determine their rotation curves. Our goals were to extend the knowledge of the dark-matter distribution to low- er luminosity systems and to constrain the phase density of their dark matter. A common problem with dwarf galaxies is that only the linear rise in rotation velocity is seen. We used a selection criterion that enhanced our chance of seeing the flat portion of the rotation curve in a system with low rota- tion velocity. We took our sample from Fisher and Tally’s catalogs (1975,1982) using only those galaxies with steep- a) Department of Physics and Astronomy, Rutgers University, P. O. Box 849, Piscataway, NJ 08854. b) National Radio Astronomical Observatory, P. O. Box O, Socorro, NM 87801. sided profiles (differential rotation?), nearly edge-on sys- tems, and small line widths corrected for inclination. We then selected the galaxies that had not yet been ob- served with a synthesis imaging instrument. The eight dwarfs were each observed with the D( 1 km) array for 1 hr. This is just sufficient to determine the extent of the gas and to get a hint of a possible turnover in the rotation curve. From position velocity profiles made along the major axis we then selected four dwarfs (DDO 52, DDO 170, DDO 181, and DDO 194), which both showed a possible turnover in the rotation curve and had H I that was extended enough to do a proper mass modeling. These candidates were observed for 3 hr each in D array in January 1986, and for 16 hr each in C ( 3 km) array in November 1986. Here we report the observations of DDO 170. We examine the implications of these observations on the distribution of dark matter. The basic halos parameters rc and vmax are bet- ter determined this way than in large galaxies. We will demonstrate that great care must be exercised in model fitting. We are interested in how the data limits pa- rameters more than what parameters fit best. Lake and Feinswog ( 1989) have shown that very few rotation curves put limits on the halo’s peak phase density. The few that do are all Sc’s and have nearly the same luminosity. II. Previous analyses (cf. Faber and Lin 1983; Kormendy 
1987) have quoted central densities of dwarf spheroidals 
that were over an order of magnitude higher than the values 
needed to explain the central velocity dispersions. The differ- 
ence is that we assume that the dwarf spheroidals reside in 
halos that are similar to those seen in DDO 170 and other 
dwarf galaxies. Prior analyses assumed that the dark matter 
is distributed like the light. The motivation for this assump- 
tion was that if the light distribution were tidally truncated, 
the dark halo would be as well. However, there would be a 
sharp decline in luminosity density as a result of imbedding

the stellar system inside the core of a dark halo (cf. Peebles 
1985 for dynamical models of globular clusters imbedded in 
such halos). Since the dark matter in large galaxies is not 
distributed like the light, it would be odd to discover that it 
was in small galaxies.

CONCLUSIONS DDO 170 is a dwarf galaxy with a luminosity of 2.3 X108 Z,0 with a rotation curve that is still weakly rising at ^:2 Holmberg radii. Using VLA and 5-band images, we built three component models of the mass distribution: a lumi- nous disk with a constant Jf/L, a gas disk whose mass is determined by the H i flux, and a dark halo. We have stressed the care that must be taken to insure that the data really constrain the model parameters. We find that: ( 1 ) the mass-to-light ratio derived from the last point of the rotation curve (12.5 kpc) is 56, (2) the ratio of gas mass (derived from the 21 cm flux) to blue luminosity is -3.7 in solar units, ( 3 ) it is the smallest galaxy where the basic halo parameters (core radius and asymptotic velocity) are determined by fitting detailed mass models, (4) it has a companion with a projected separation of 62 kpc and a line- of-sight velocity difference of 85 km s - ^ The 7 = 2 models span a range from the “maximal halo” model with rc = 1.9 kpc, ymax = 71 kms”1 through the “maximal disk” model with rc =4.1 kpc, umax = 79 km s - *. In the best-fit model of the rotation curve, the halo param- eters are rc = 2.4 kpc, ymax = 73 km s_I. Maximizing the contribution of the disk to the rotation curve, pushes rc and i^max t0 large values and leads to larger halo masses when extrapolated to large radii. In all of our models, at least half of the “baryonic” mass of this galaxy is in the form of gas. 560 The central density of the halo, its density at the Holm- berg radius, and the ratio of dark-to-light mass at the Holm- berg radius are slightly higher than the values found for bright galaxies. An extrapolation of the L~v relation for bright disk galaxies (L cc y^x ) correctly predicts the value at the Holmberg radius. The velocity at the last measured point on the rotation curve and the velocity difference between DDO 170 and its companion support the L oc Ay8 scaling found for the velocity differences in binary pairs of galaxies. We used the companion to get a mass estimate in three ways. The minimum binding mass is 5.2 X 1010 ^0. The use of a standard statistical mass estimator raises this to 5.2X 1011 JtQ. While the luminosity of DDO 170 is less than 1 % of L* (the characteristic luminosity defined by the luminosity function), its total mass is nearly the same. The constraints on the halo parameters (rc and ymax) placed by our models of the rotation curve are robust to gross changes in our models and represent the best current limits on the phase density of dark matter. The mass of this component is determined using the 21 cm flux. However, the dynamical mass varies as one power of the distance while the gas mass goes as the distance squared. Lake ( 1989a) found that if the distance is as large as 10 Mpc (Huchtmeier and Seiradakis 1985; Krumm and Burstein 1984) or if the mass in molecular gas were ~ 1.4 times that in H I, the rotation curve could be fit without any dark matter. Indeed, such models fit better than those with dark matter. A more accurate distance measurement would help remove some of the ambiguities. Whatever the out- come, DDO 154 is a most interesting system. b) The Dwarf Spheroidals In the dwarf spheroidals, dark matter can be probed by measuring the velocity dispersion of a few stars. ( Aaronson 1983). Results have accrued for Fornax, Sculptor, and Car- ina (Seitzer and Frogel 1985 ) as well as for Ursa Minor and Draco (Aaronson and Olszewski 1986). The central density in the best-fit model for DDO 170isl.7xl0-2 pc _ 3. If the dwarf spheroidals are imbedded in halos with this den- sity, the one-dimensional velocity dispersion of a tracer pop- ulation would be ~ 21 km s~ ^ where rh is the mean radi- us of tracer population. Over the full range of our halo models, the dispersions would be —10-27 rh km s~K Since the tracers in the dwarfs have ~0.4 kpc, then we expect <7~ 10 + 5, in fair agreement with the observations (Aaron- son and Olszewski 1986). Previous analyses (cf. Faber and Lin 1983; Kormendy 1987) have quoted central densities of dwarf spheroidals that were over an order of magnitude higher than the values needed to explain the central velocity dispersions. The differ- ence is that we assume that the dwarf spheroidals reside in halos that are similar to those seen in DDO 170 and other dwarf galaxies. Prior analyses assumed that the dark matter is distributed like the light. The motivation for this assump- tion was that if the light distribution were tidally truncated, the dark halo would be as well. However, there would be a sharp decline in luminosity density as a result of imbedding the stellar system inside the core of a dark halo (cf. P. 6128, Suce. A, Montréal, Québec, H3C 3J7, Canada Received 19 April 1990; revised 1 June 1990 ABSTRACT New optical and radio observations of NGC 3109 (DDO 236) are presented. From the surface photom- etry in the / band, a scale length a-1 = 3.11' is found for the exponential disk. Comparison with previously published B photometry shows that the surface color remains nearly constant with radius out to 11'. Radio synthesis imaging in the H I spectral line reveals a gaseous envelope 40'X 12' in size. The H I distribution is severely warped in the outer parts, with a — 5-kpc-long appendage on the southwest side. A tilted ring model of the observed velocity field yields a slowly rising rotation curve; neither the turnover point nor the flat portion are reached with the present observations. The maximum rotational velocity is only -¿67 kms-1 at the last measured point of the rotation curve. Studying the mass distribution, a “no dark-matter” model with constant maximum {<^/LB)* = 1.1 for the stellar disk and including the distribution of the H I fails to reproduce the observed rotation curve. Combining the luminous matter with a dark, isothermal halo, gives {^/LB)* =0.5 + 0.2 for the disk, and a core radius rc = 6.7 + 0.7 kpc with a one-dimensional velocity dispersion (j = 47.0 + 2.0 km s-1 for the halo component. While those two parameters are not well constrained, the central density of the halo Pq~0.008 + 0.001 pc-3 is much better defined. At the last measured point of the rotation curve, NGC 3109 is entirely dominated by dark matter. In fact, the contribution from the dark component dominates at nearly all radii; for this system, there is clearly no “disk-halo conspiracy.” Finally, it is shown that for NGC 3109, the H I gas traces the dark matter distribution very well. I. INTRODUCTION The most convincing evidence for the existence of large halos of unseen matter has come in recent years from the study of the H I kinematics and the mass modeling of spiral galaxies (Carignan and Freeman 1985; van Albada and Sancisi 1986; Kent 1987; Carignan and Freeman 1988; Lake and Feins wog 1989). No directly observable component, be it stellar or gaseous, can produce the potential needed to account for the leveling off of rotation curves at large galac- tocentric distances now seen in a majority of spirals through H I observations. Detailed mass models are interesting for determining dark halo parameters and hence study how they scale with other large-scale properties of galaxies, such as type, mass, and luminosity (Kormendy 1988). The same parameters can help to establish limits (e.g., neutrino phase- space constraint: Tremaine and Gunn 1979; Lake 1989) on the possible nature of dark matter, which still remains un- known. Late-type spirals are good candidates for this purpose: the absence of bulge reduces the number of free parameters in the models and thus the uncertainties on the derived param- eters. As new 21 cm observations are made, it turns out that these galaxies are very often gas-rich systems, in which the H I component can be dynamically as important as the stel- lar disk itself (Carignan and Beaulieu 1989). Thus the pre- cise modeling of these galaxies requires high-quality mea- surements of the kinematics and distribution of the H I gas. Mass models of the Magellanic-type spiral NGC 3109 were already presented by Carignan ( 1985a,b) using a rota- tion curve based on low-resolution, single-dish observations. The precise H i radial distribution was unknown. In this paper, we propose to use high-resolution synthesis observa- tions to provide the necessary kinematics and distribution of the H I gas. /-band photometry, performed in order to deter- mine the distribution of the old stellar disk population, more representative of the true mass distribution of the disk, will be compared to the i?-band photometry. The optical and radio observations are presented in Sec. II. In Sec. Ill, the luminosity profile is extracted from the optical data, while the H I properties of NGC 3109 are examined in Sec. IV. The plate was digitized using the University of Toronto PDS microdensitometer in density mode, with an aperture of 50pm and step size of 50pm, for a total of 1024 X 1024 pixels. The original plate scale of 67.12 arcsec mm"1 thus gives 3.36 arcsec on a side for each pixel. The calibration spots were also scanned using the same procedure. Because of a serious amount of diffusion within the emulsion, the less exposed spots were contaminated by light from the more exposed ones. In an attempt to compen- sate for this effect, we subtracted from every spot a surface that was fitted through its immediate surroundings; this pro- cedure also subtracted the plate fog, a side effect we had to take into account in the next steps. P. 6128, Suce. A, Montréal, Québec, H3C 3J7, Canada Received 19 April 1990; revised 1 June 1990 ABSTRACT New optical and radio observations of NGC 3109 (DDO 236) are presented. From the surface photom- etry in the / band, a scale length a-1 = 3.11' is found for the exponential disk. Comparison with previously published B photometry shows that the surface color remains nearly constant with radius out to 11'. Radio synthesis imaging in the H I spectral line reveals a gaseous envelope 40'X 12' in size. The H I distribution is severely warped in the outer parts, with a — 5-kpc-long appendage on the southwest side. A tilted ring model of the observed velocity field yields a slowly rising rotation curve; neither the turnover point nor the flat portion are reached with the present observations. The maximum rotational velocity is only -¿67 kms-1 at the last measured point of the rotation curve. Studying the mass distribution, a “no dark-matter” model with constant maximum {<^/LB)* = 1.1 for the stellar disk and including the distribution of the H I fails to reproduce the observed rotation curve. Combining the luminous matter with a dark, isothermal halo, gives {^/LB)* =0.5 + 0.2 for the disk, and a core radius rc = 6.7 + 0.7 kpc with a one-dimensional velocity dispersion (j = 47.0 + 2.0 km s-1 for the halo component. While those two parameters are not well constrained, the central density of the halo Pq~0.008 + 0.001 pc-3 is much better defined. At the last measured point of the rotation curve, NGC 3109 is entirely dominated by dark matter. In fact, the contribution from the dark component dominates at nearly all radii; for this system, there is clearly no “disk-halo conspiracy.” Finally, it is shown that for NGC 3109, the H I gas traces the dark matter distribution very well. I. INTRODUCTION The most convincing evidence for the existence of large halos of unseen matter has come in recent years from the study of the H I kinematics and the mass modeling of spiral galaxies (Carignan and Freeman 1985; van Albada and Sancisi 1986; Kent 1987; Carignan and Freeman 1988; Lake and Feins wog 1989). No directly observable component, be it stellar or gaseous, can produce the potential needed to account for the leveling off of rotation curves at large galac- tocentric distances now seen in a majority of spirals through H I observations. Detailed mass models are interesting for determining dark halo parameters and hence study how they scale with other large-scale properties of galaxies, such as type, mass, and luminosity (Kormendy 1988). The same parameters can help to establish limits (e.g., neutrino phase- space constraint: Tremaine and Gunn 1979; Lake 1989) on the possible nature of dark matter, which still remains un- known. Late-type spirals are good candidates for this purpose: the absence of bulge reduces the number of free parameters in the models and thus the uncertainties on the derived param- eters. As new 21 cm observations are made, it turns out that these galaxies are very often gas-rich systems, in which the H I component can be dynamically as important as the stel- lar disk itself (Carignan and Beaulieu 1989). Thus the pre- cise modeling of these galaxies requires high-quality mea- surements of the kinematics and distribution of the H I gas. Mass models of the Magellanic-type spiral NGC 3109 were already presented by Carignan ( 1985a,b) using a rota- tion curve based on low-resolution, single-dish observations. The precise H i radial distribution was unknown. In this paper, we propose to use high-resolution synthesis observa- tions to provide the necessary kinematics and distribution of the H I gas. /-band photometry, performed in order to deter- mine the distribution of the old stellar disk population, more repr

1990AJ 100. . 648J 649 M. JOBIN AND C. CARIGNAN: NGC 3109 649 overexposed stars, which would have made the fitting proce- dure all the more difficult and uncertain, were removed. The fitted background was subtracted from the calibrated frame, and the resulting image was divided by the same background frame. From the surface photom- etry in the / band, a scale length a-1 = 3.11' is found for the exponential disk. Comparison with previously published B photometry shows that the surface color remains nearly constant with radius out to 11'. Radio synthesis imaging in the H I spectral line reveals a gaseous envelope 40'X 12' in size. The H I distribution is severely warped in the outer parts, with a — 5-kpc-long appendage on the southwest side. A tilted ring model of the observed velocity field yields a slowly rising rotation curve; neither the turnover point nor the flat portion are reached with the present observations. The maximum rotational velocity is only -¿67 kms-1 at the last measured point of the rotation curve. Studying the mass distribution, a “no dark-matter” model with constant maximum {<^/LB)* = 1.1 for the stellar disk and including the distribution of the H I fails to reproduce the observed rotation curve. Combining the luminous matter with a dark, isothermal halo, gives {^/LB)* =0.5 + 0.2 for the disk, and a core radius rc = 6.7 + 0.7 kpc with a one-dimensional velocity dispersion (j = 47.0 + 2.0 km s-1 for the halo component. While those two parameters are not well constrained, the central density of the halo Pq~0.008 + 0.001 pc-3 is much better defined. At the last measured point of the rotation curve, NGC 3109 is entirely dominated by dark matter. In fact, the contribution from the dark component dominates at nearly all radii; for this system, there is clearly no “disk-halo conspiracy.” Finally, it is shown that for NGC 3109, the H I gas traces the dark matter distribution very well. I. INTRODUCTION The most convincing evidence for the existence of large halos of unseen matter has come in recent years from the study of the H I kinematics and the mass modeling of spiral galaxies (Carignan and Freeman 1985; van Albada and Sancisi 1986; Kent 1987; Carignan and Freeman 1988; Lake and Feins wog 1989). No directly observable component, be it stellar or gaseous, can produce the potential needed to account for the leveling off of rotation curves at large galac- tocentric distances now seen in a majority of spirals through H I observations. Detailed mass models are interesting for determining dark halo parameters and hence study how they scale with other large-scale properties of galaxies, such as type, mass, and luminosity (Kormendy 1988). The same parameters can help to establish limits (e.g., neutrino phase- space constraint: Tremaine and Gunn 1979; Lake 1989) on the possible nature of dark matter, which still remains un- known. Late-type spirals are good candidates for this purpose: the absence of bulge reduces the number of free parameters in the models and thus the uncertainties on the derived param- eters. As new 21 cm observations are made, it turns out that these galaxies are very often gas-rich systems, in which the H I component can be dynamically as important as the stel- lar disk itself (Carignan and Beaulieu 1989). Thus the pre- cise modeling of these galaxies requires high-quality mea- surements of the kinematics and distribution of the H I gas. Mass models of the Magellanic-type spiral NGC 3109 were already presented by Carignan ( 1985a,b) using a rota- tion curve based on low-resolution, single-dish observations. The precise H i radial distribution was unknown. In this paper, we propose to use high-resolution synthesis observa- tions to provide the necessary kinematics and distribution of the H I gas. /-band photometry, performed in order to deter- mine the distribution of the old stellar disk population, more representative of the true mass distribution of the disk, will be compared to the i?-band photometry. The optical and radio observations are presented in Sec. II. In Sec. Ill, the luminosity profile is extracted from the optical data, while the H I properties of NGC 3109 are examined in Sec. IV. Section V discusses the formalism used for the mass models and presents the results which are then analyzed in Sec. VI. II. OBSERVATIONS a) Optical A IV-N (/ band) plate, taken by the staff at the U. K. Schmidt Telescope Unit, served as the basis for the surface photometry of NGC 3109. The plate was digitized using the University of Toronto PDS microdensitometer in density mode, with an aperture of 50pm and step size of 50pm, for a total of 1024 X 1024 pixels. The original plate scale of 67.12 arcsec mm"1 thus gives 3.36 arcsec on a side for each pixel. The calibration spots were also scanned using the same procedure. Because of a serious amount of diffusion within the emulsion, the less exposed spots were contaminated by light from the more exposed ones. In an attempt to compen- sate for this effect, we subtracted from every spot a surface that was fitted through its immediate surroundings; this pro- cedure also subtracted the plate fog, a side effect we had to take into account in the next steps. THE ASTRONOMICAL JOURNAL VOLUME 95, NUMBER 1 JANUARY 1988 LO CT) Hi AND MASS DISTRIBUTION IN THE DWARF “REGULAR” GALAXY UGC 2259 Claude Carignan Département de Physique, Observatoire du Mont Mégantic, Université de Montréal, Montréal, Québec H3C 3J7, Canada Renzo Sancisi and Tjeerd S. van Aleada Kapteyn Astronomical Institute, Postbus 800, 9700 AV, Groningen, The Netherlands Received 19 February 1987; revised 24 September 1987 ABSTRACT H i synthesis observations of the dwarf “regular” galaxy UGC 2259 are presented. This system has a symmetrical H I distribution extending over 2D25 and a regular velocity field which shows no sign of departure from axial symmetry. It is therefore most suitable for studying the mass distribution in late- type spirals. Despite the fact that UGC 2259 is fainter than most other objects of the same morphologi- cal type, its H i properties are typical of an Scd galaxy. While other low-luminosity galaxies studied so far in H i exhibit solid-body type rotation curves, this dwarf system has a flat rotation curve similar to what is seen in more luminous spirals. The main difference between UGC 2259 and other low-luminosi- ty galaxies is its regular appearance. Studying the mass distribution, it is found that a “minimum” dark isothermal halo with one-dimensional velocity dispersion a =55 km s-1 and core radius rc =5.5 kpc is needed to reproduce the observed rotation curve. In this case, the dark halo and the luminous disk contribute about equally to the circular velocity at the Holmberg radius. However, because the rotation curve is still slightly rising in the outer parts, the halo parameters are not as constrained as in the case of an exactly flat rotation curve. This result, by extending the luminosity range of well-studied galaxies, strengthens earlier suggestions that the ratio of dark to luminous matter is independent of galaxy luminosity. I. INTRODUCTION The study of the ratio of dark to luminous matter in spiral galaxies has been the subject of several recent studies (Bah- call 1983; Casertano 1983; Carignan and Freeman 1985; van Albada et al. 1985; Carignan 1985; Athanassoula et al. 1987). These studies have been possible because of the large number of high-sensitivity H I observations that became available in the last few years, allowing the halo potential to be probed to large galactocentric distances. In the case of NGC 3198 (van Albada et al. 1985), it was even possible to derive the rotation curve out to 11 disk scale lengths. One of the important questions, forming the motivation for this type of work, is whether the properties of dark halos are a function of galaxy type or luminosity. For example, does dark matter scale with luminous matter or does the ratio of dark to luminous matter, inside an isophotal radius, increase along the Hubble sequence when going from lumi- nous Sc’s to low-luminosity late-type systems (Tinsley 1981; Faber 1982; Vader 1984)? So far, a modest range of luminosities has been studied, from Mb = — 21 to MB = — 18. Within the uncertainties of the mass models, no trend with galaxy luminosity has been found. Ratios of dark to luminous matter vary from 0.5 to 1.5 at the Holmberg radius (Faber 1982; Carignan and Freeman 1985). The obvious next step is to extend this kind of study to lower-luminosity systems. However, in most of the fainter systems (MB > — 17) studied so far, the flattened part of the rotation curve is rarely reached (Tully et al. 1978 ). Instead, these galaxies exhibit solid-body type rotation curves which do not allow constraint of the parameters of the mass mod- els. Another problem sometimes encountered with low-lu- minosity systems is that their velocity fields show departures from axial symmetry that make the interpretation uncertain. It should be noted that most of those low-luminosity sys- tems are irregulars. One of the starting points of this project was to see if the situation would be different with low-lumi- nosity regular galaxies, provided one could find such objects. Some years ago, Tully (1975) pointed out such a system: UGC 2259. He described it as the intrinsically smallest known grand-design spiral (MB ~ — 16). Its regular two- arm spiral pattern is clearly seen in Fig. 1 [Plate 1]. On account of these properties, UGC 2259 was observed in the 21cm line of H i with the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Tele- scope (WSRT) and optically with the 1.6 m telescope of L’Observatoire du Mont Mégantic. The optical parameters of UGC 2259 are given in Table I. It is possibly a member of the NGC 1023/NGC 1058 group. For this study, a distance of 7.33 Mpc is adopted, based on its redshift and HQ= 100 km s-1 Mpc-1. It is not known whether the dwarf elliptical 1!5 to the northeast is a close companion since no redshift is available for this system. CCD on the 1.6 m telescope. With 30 fim pixels, the resolu- 
tion was —0.5 arcsec/pixel and the scale 16.0 arcsec/mm. 
The seeing (FWHM) during the observations was —2.5 arc- 
sec. The magnitude scales were determined by observing a 
standard field in M67 (Schild 1983) . Separate “blank” fields

SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS A study of the H I and mass distribution for the dwarf “regular” galaxy UGC 2259 has been presented. The main results from the WSRT observations are: (i) The H I content of UGC 2259 is typical of that found in more luminous Scd galaxies. A total H i mass of 2.4 X 108 ^0 is derived which corresponds to a ^H/L5 = 0.42. (ii) The distribution of H i surface densities is found to be nearly constant out to ~D25 before starting to decrease. At a level of 5 X 1019 cm-2, the HI extends over more than 2Z>25. (iii) The H i velocity field is regular. No systematic vari- ation of the orientation parameters with radius is found. Constant values of / = 41°, P.A. = 160°, and Vsys =582 km s -1 are adopted. (iv) The most remarkable result for this low-luminosity galaxy is that the shape of its rotation curve is similar to that seen in more luminous spirals ( Rubin et al. 1980; Sancisi and van Albada 1986), while the rotational velocities on the ris- ing branch agree with those predicted for a low-luminosity Sc spiral (Rubinetal. 1985). The rotation curve rises slowly ( ~2 km s-1 kpc-1) between 2 and 7 kpc. Constraints on the orientation parameters are such that a flat rotation curve is marginally acceptable, but a Keplerian decrease can be excluded. Using the rotation curve derived from the H i observa- tions, the maximum-disk-mass model yields the following results: (i) Contrary to other low-luminosity galaxies, the H I component of UGC 2259 is not dynamically significant with a 1 /^disk of only 0.08. (ii) In order to reproduce the observed rotation curve, a “minimum” isothermal halo with a =55 kms-1 and rc = 5.5 kpc must be added to the stellar disk (^disk = 3.2X109 ^0). This implies a central density for the halo ofp0 = 0.017 pc-3. (iii) If smaller disks are allowed, the limits on the core radius of the halo become 1.6<a*c <5.5 kpc. (iv) The luminous disk and the dark halo contribute al- most equal amounts of mass at the Holmberg radius. The latter result is similar to that found in more luminous galaxies and is consistent with conclusions reached by Fall and Efstathiou ( 1980) studying a sample of spirals covering morphological types from Sa to Sm. Conversely, we find no evidence for the suggestion by Tinsley ( 1981 ) that the ratio of nonluminous to luminous matter inside the Holmberg ra- dius is a function of galaxy Hubble type (within the range of spiral types covered by H i rotation curves from Sb to Sm). THE ASTRONOMICAL JOURNAL VOLUME 95, NUMBER 1 JANUARY 1988 LO CT) Hi AND MASS DISTRIBUTION IN THE DWARF “REGULAR” GALAXY UGC 2259 Claude Carignan Département de Physique, Observatoire du Mont Mégantic, Université de Montréal, Montréal, Québec H3C 3J7, Canada Renzo Sancisi and Tjeerd S. van Aleada Kapteyn Astronomical Institute, Postbus 800, 9700 AV, Groningen, The Netherlands Received 19 February 1987; revised 24 September 1987 ABSTRACT H i synthesis observations of the dwarf “regular” galaxy UGC 2259 are presented. This system has a symmetrical H I distribution extending over 2D25 and a regular velocity field which shows no sign of departure from axial symmetry. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS A study of the H I and mass distribution for the dwarf “regular” galaxy UGC 2259 has been presented. The main results from the WSRT observations are: (i) The H I content of UGC 2259 is typical of that found in more luminous Scd galaxies. A total H i mass of 2.4 X 108 ^0 is derived which corresponds to a ^H/L5 = 0.42. (ii) The distribution of H i surface densities is found to be nearly constant out to ~D25 before starting to decrease. At a level of 5 X 1019 cm-2, the HI extends over more than 2Z>25. (iii) The H i velocity field is regular. No systematic vari- ation of the orientation parameters with radius is found. Constant values of / = 41°, P.A. = 160°, and Vsys =582 km s -1 are adopted. (iv) The most remarkable result for this low-luminosity galaxy is that the shape of its rotation curve is similar to that seen in more luminous spirals ( Rubin et al. 1980; Sancisi and van Albada 1986), while the rotational velocities on the ris- ing branch agree with those predicted for a low-luminosity Sc spiral (Rubinetal. 1985). The rotation curve rises slowly ( ~2 km s-1 kpc-1) between 2 and 7 kpc. Constraints on the orientation parameters are such that a flat rotation curve is marginally acceptable, but a Keplerian decrease can be excluded. Using the rotation curve derived from the H i observa- tions, the maximum-disk-mass model yields the following results: (i) Contrary to other low-luminosity galaxies, the H I component of UGC 2259 is not dynamically significant with a 1 /^disk of only 0.08. (ii) In order to reproduce the observed rotation curve, a “minimum” isothermal halo with a =55 kms-1 and rc = 5.5 kpc must be added to the stellar disk (^disk = 3.2X109 ^0). This implies a central density for the halo ofp0 = 0.017 pc-3. (iii) If smaller disks are allowed, the limits on the core radius of the halo become 1.6<a*c <5.5 kpc. (iv) The luminous disk and the dark halo contribute al- most equal amounts of mass at the Holmberg radius. The latter result is similar to that found in more luminous galaxies and is consistent with conclusions reached by Fall and Efstathiou ( 1980) studying a sample of spirals covering morphological types from Sa to Sm. Conversely, we find no evidence for the suggestion by Tinsley ( 1981 ) that the ratio of nonluminous to luminous matter inside the Holmberg ra- dius is a function of galaxy Hubble type (within the range of spiral types covered by H i rotation curves from Sb to Sm). The next step was to obtain a least-squares solution for P.A., /, and KROt (rotational velocities) after dividing the data in 20" rings in the plane of the galaxy. The data in an opening angle of 90° about the minor axis (in the plane of the galaxy) were excluded from the analysis. As expected from the shape of the isovelocity contours, no systematic trend was seen and constant values of P.A. = 160° and / = 41° were adopted. The uncertainties in position angle and incli- nation for individual rings are Io and 3°, respectively (1er). The derived parameters are summarized in Table III. The rotation curve can now be obtained using the above fixed values for the orientation parameters. The rotation curve was also derived separately for the northern and southern halves of the galaxy. The differences between the two halves are of order 1-3 km s~1, except in the inner 40", where they reach about 6 km s-1. We have superposed, in Fig. 7, our adopted rotation curve onto a position-velocity plot taken along the major axis. It can be seen that the rotation curve is a good representation of the velocities on both sides of the galaxy. Finally, beam-smearing corrections were calculated but were found negligible. Another way to check whether the adopted rotation curve is consistent with the velocity field is to construct a model velocity field and to look at the residuals after subtracting the model from the observed velocity field. These residuals are almost everywhere less than 5 km s-1, with very few of order 10 km s~ ^ The only apparent noncircular motions are along the minor axis on the west side, but the amplitude is small (<10km s-1). However, before doing this, it is worth asking how certain one can be of the general shape of the rotation curve, and in particular of the gentle rise in the outer parts. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS A study of the H I and mass distribution for the dwarf “regular” galaxy UGC 2259 has been presented. The main results from the WSRT observations are: (i) The H I content of UGC 2259 is typical of that found in more luminous Scd galaxies. A total H i mass of 2.4 X 108 ^0 is derived which corresponds to a ^H/L5 = 0.42. (ii) The distribution of H i surface densities is found to be nearly constant out to ~D25 before starting to decrease. At a level of 5 X 1019 cm-2, the HI extends over more than 2Z>25. (iii) The H i velocity field is regular. No systematic vari- ation of the orientation parameters with radius is found. Constant values of / = 41°, P.A. = 160°, and Vsys =582 km s -1 are adopted. (iv) The most remarkable result for this low-luminosity galaxy is that the shape of its rotation curve is similar to that seen in more luminous spirals ( Rubin et al. 1980; Sancisi and van Albada 1986), while the rotational velocities on the ris- ing branch agree with those predicted for a low-luminosity Sc spiral (Rubinetal. 1985). The rotation curve rises slowly ( ~2 km s-1 kpc-1) between 2 and 7 kpc. Constraints on the orientation parameters are such that a flat rotation curve is marginally acceptable, but a Keplerian decrease can be excluded. Using the rotation curve derived from the H i observa- tions, the maximum-disk-mass model yields the following results: (i) Contrary to other low-luminosity galaxies, the H I component of UGC 2259 is not dynamically significant with a 1 /^disk of only 0.08. (ii) In order to reproduce the observed rotation curve, a “minimum” isothermal halo with a =55 kms-1 and rc = 5.5 kpc must be added to the stellar disk (^disk = 3.2X109 ^0). This implies a central density for the halo ofp0 = 0.017 pc-3. (iii) If smaller disks are allowed, the limits on the core radius of the halo become 1.6<a*c <5.5 kpc. (iv) The luminous disk and the dark halo contribute al- most equal amounts of mass at the Holmberg radius. The latter result is similar to that found in more luminous galaxies and is consistent with conclusions reached by Fall and Efstathiou ( 1980) studying a sample of spirals covering morphological types from Sa to Sm. Conversely, we find no evidence for the suggestion by Tinsley ( 1981 ) that the ratio of nonluminous to luminous matter inside the Holmberg ra- dius is a function of galaxy Hubble type (within the range of spiral types covered by H i rotation curves from Sb to Sm).
